is an independent flow of execution with its own stack and saved registers. On bare metal there is no OS to create it: we build the data structures ourselves. This page covers the task control block, the task stack taken from the

Giving every task its own stack on

Allocating the stack from the heap
A heap-allocated stack has no guard page: if the task uses more than you gave it, it silently overwrites the next heap block. See stack overflow detection below.
A new task has never run, so nothing was ever saved for it. We

it was interrupted just before its first instruction: we build, by hand, the same frame the hardware and the PendSV handler would have pushed. The first context switch to the task then "returns" into its entry function.

uint32_t *build_initial_frame(uint32_t *sp, void (*entry)(void *), void *arg)
{
  *--sp = 0x01000000u;                              /* xPSR: Thumb bit (T) set */
  *--sp = ((uint32_t)entry) & 0xFFFFFFFEu;          /* PC  : task entry        */
  *--sp = (uint32_t)task_exit;                      /* LR  : if entry returns  */
  *--sp = 0;                                        /* R12 */
  *--sp = 0; *--sp = 0; *--sp = 0;                  /* R3, R2, R1 */
  *--sp = (uint32_t)arg;                            /* R0  : first argument    */
  for (int r = 11; r >= 4; r--) { *--sp = 0; }      /* R11..R4 (software part) */
  return sp;                                        /* saved into tcb->sp */
}
R4 R5 R6 R7 R8 R9 R10 R11
Sources: Cortex-M exception entry stacks xPSR, PC, LR, R12, R3–R0 and the handler saves R4–R11 (
). I did not find ARM's own manual page in my search: for authoritative details check the ARMv7-M Architecture Reference Manual.

PendSV_Handler:
    mrs   r0, psp
    stmdb r0!, {r4-r11}         @ save R4-R11 below the hardware frame
    ldr   r1, =current_tcb
    ldr   r2, [r1]
    str   r0, [r2]              @ current->sp = psp
    push  {r1, lr}              @ keep r1 and EXC_RETURN across the call
    bl    sched_pick_next       @ returns the next tcb in r0
    pop   {r1, lr}
    str   r0, [r1]              @ current_tcb = next
    ldr   r0, [r0]              @ r0 = next->sp
    ldmia r0!, {r4-r11}         @ restore R4-R11
    msr   psp, r0
    bx    lr                    @ EXC_RETURN 0xFFFFFFFD: thread mode, use PSP

(released) and let the pull-up raise the line.

Simplified: this ignores clock stretching (a real driver waits for SCL to actually go high) and the delays need tuning for your CPU speed and the bus speed you want. It is for learning how the signals are made.
Pins the hardware peripheral cannot reach.
Quick bring-up and debugging of a new device.
Never in a timing-critical system: interrupts and task switches stretch the delays.

children.title: Revise: UART vs SPI vs I2C

content.text: SCLK, MOSI, MISO + CS per slave
up to a few Mbit/s (set by baud)

UART frames each byte with start/stop bits and needs matching baud rates. SPI shifts bits in both directions on a shared clock and picks the slave with CS. I2C shares two open-drain wires and picks the device by an address, with an ACK after every byte.
"SPI has addresses" (no, it has chip select); "I2C is full duplex" (no); "UART has a clock" (no); "pull-ups are optional on I2C" (no).
I can draw a UART 8N1 frame and explain a framing error
I can explain SPI modes 0–3 and chip select
I can explain I2C addressing, ACK, START/STOP and repeated START
I can say why I2C needs pull-ups
I can pick the right bus for a given requirement
